# R272 — Xe verifier device-clock profile scope and safe use

Date: 2026-10-12  
Status: source-only audit; no code changed and no GPU, build, test, profiler, or active-run inspection was performed.

## Scope and evidence

Audited WN0691 source at `/home/yayoi/ghq/github.com/yqYo1/Strata/.worktree/sync-xe-v0143-nonfinite-20261012` (the current 0691 Xe worktree), focusing on `src/core/verify.cpp`, `src/kernels/xe/verify_kernels.cpp`, `src/kernels/xe/fused_gr.cpp`, and the verifier headers. Read only the closed receipt `main-decode-criticalpath-model-root-v1/xe-timed1-on/record.json`; did not inspect the concurrently active Main process or logs.

The closed receipt records 16 one-token windows at 124.09 ms/window: verify 121.44 ms, including GPU-reach wait 50.27 ms, per-layer host 55.16 ms (CPU 50.64 ms), stage 0.49 ms, and commit/emit 2.65 ms. It has `decode_gpu_stage_lines: []`. It is not a profile-enabled measurement; it gives no device-stage breakdown and cannot calibrate the profile clock. Its input context was 32K while the model context limit remained 262,144. Receipt SHA-256: `de826d6cd915b121801ebb3ba5d5f86f0945d82ae6f0819a59bc974c094b71dc`.

## What the switch measures

`STRATA_VERIFY_PROFILE` is enabled by environment-variable presence. On Xe, availability requires both compile-time `SYCL_EXT_ONEAPI_CLOCK` and runtime `aspect::ext_oneapi_clock_device`; otherwise the profile logs that it is off. Device allocation failure also disables it. The supported CUDA path instead reads NVPTX `%globaltimer`, documented in source as nanoseconds, but that is not the Xe code path.

The Xe implementation submits a one-work-item `single_task` for each stamp and stores `sycl::ext::oneapi::experimental::clock<clock_scope::device>()`. WN comments explicitly say the tick frequency is not established. Intel’s extension specification describes these values as monotonic counter samples whose rate may vary, and states there is no portable conversion to elapsed time. It also says current Intel GPU devices support only the subgroup clock aspect; therefore the runtime device-aspect check must decide whether this Xe build can profile on the actual Arc B570. Do not assume the experimental device-scope aspect is available on that GPU based only on compiler support.

For each recorded layer, the regular points are slot 0, 1–14, 16–24 (slot 15 is unused), plus internal fused mixer points in slots 27 onward. These are deltas between adjacent stamps and can include several kernels, graph/command scheduling, or queue idle periods; labels are scope names, not per-kernel timings:

- 1 `hc-read0`; 2 `q8+qkv/q-idx gemv`; 3–6 `conv`, `ab`, `z`, `rec`; 7 `q8+kv-idx`; 8 `k/v+norm-rope`; 9 `kv+idx append`; 10 `q+q-idx`; 11 `scores+topk`; 12 `kv-resolve`; 13 `attention`; 14 `gate`; 16 `out-proj`.
- 17 `hc-read1+router`; 18 `shared+quant`; 19 `waitA`; 20 `VRAM hits`; 21 `waitB`; 22 `PCIe grp`; 23 `waitCPU`; 24 `copy+combine`. The stage route and kernel choices determine what work falls inside these broad spans. In particular they do not isolate every dense/GDN/QSA/shared-expert kernel.
- 25 `(gap)` is the interval from one layer’s slot 24 to the next layer’s slot 0, accumulated only between layers in the current stage. It may include device-idle time and, in segmented mode, host service and relaunch delay. It is not a pure GPU compute duration or the total graph tail.
- 26 `head` is slot 0 to slot 1 for the final stage: it encloses the output head, greedy sampler and optional non-finite scan. It is not a head-kernel-only measurement. There is no final stamp after slot 1, graph completion, or the subsequent stream synchronization and host work.
- 27–29 split the initial fused hyper-connection read interval into norm/down/up when the internal stamps are valid. They are subcomponents of slot 1, and the aggregate subtracts that outer span before reporting subdivisions. Internal stamp slots 30–32 belong to the second mixer half/adjacent-layer arrangement; absent points are skipped.

The report sums accumulated device-clock differences by GDN/QSA layer class, divides by 1,000,000, and labels the result “M ticks/window.” It accumulates until `profile_report()` prints and resets the sums. This formatting is not a unit conversion to ms. The profile buffer is zeroed at verifier initialization; window stamps are copied back after the ordinary compute and copy streams complete. Missing/out-of-order stamps are ignored. In pipelined mode, pinned host storage is allocated only if available, the async stamp copy is issued on the compute stream, and accumulation occurs after the completion event; when that host allocation fails, pipelined windows are unprofiled. Destruction synchronizes compute and copy streams before releasing the device/profile and pinned buffers.

## Graph, segmented execution, and perturbation

Stamps are submitted on the compute queue while `record_window()` is capturing the repeated window graph. Thus every stamp becomes another captured command/node (one small single-task command, not a host synchronization per point). A one-token layer has 25 ordinary stamp points plus internal fused-mixer samples where the selected implementation provides them; the final head adds two. Across a deep model this is a large node-count increase. Its device execution and graph scheduling overhead are uncalibrated here and can change observed stage durations.

Profiling also changes the computation schedule: `br`, the mixer side branch selected by `STRATA_DF_BRANCH`, requires `!prof_on_`. Enabling the profile therefore suppresses that overlap branch. This is another reason to treat the profile as a diagnostic arm and compare it with unprofiled, same-context wall-clock receipts.

Segmented capture does not disable stamps. It cuts the captured graph at host-service boundaries, then the host synchronizes the compute segment, services CPU expert work, drains the copy queue and launches the next segment. Stamps around device phases remain recorded, but the 25 gap can span those host-controlled intervals; the profile has no host clock stamps. On non-segmented execution, `waitA`, `waitB`, and `waitCPU` represent device-side wait spans around host-published flags. In segmented mode, equivalent handoffs are completed between graph launches, so those device-wait spans can be absent or changed. The runtime safety gate may force segmented mode when concurrent host/device handoff is not qualified; setting `STRATA_VERIFY_SEGMENTED=0` cannot bypass that gate. The closed receipt shows segmented mode on and profile lines absent; it remains a clean unprofiled wall measurement.

The host `run()` path waits for the whole compute stream and copy stream after the final captured stamp. The profile’s final point is before those waits and before host-side postprocessing. It consequently under-measures final graph tail/queue completion and does not attribute the reported wall-time 50.27 ms GPU-reach wait or 50.64 ms CPU service as a wall-time breakdown. The large `head` span does cover its device head work, but has no matching end-of-graph marker.

## Safe minimal diagnostic use

1. Keep the current quiet `STRATA_DECODE_TIMING` arm unprofiled. For a diagnostic run only, enable `STRATA_VERIFY_PROFILE` for a small fixed set of one-token windows, preserve the same 32K prompt, 262,144 max context, weights, route, and segmentation mode, and verify the startup output confirms the stage profile is actually on. Record the exact backend/compiler/device and runtime aspect result; if unsupported, stop treating this switch as available rather than changing timing systems mid-comparison.
2. Use the readout only to rank broad within-window spans and compare deltas from the same device/build/configuration. Do not convert M ticks to milliseconds, infer per-kernel latency from the labels, subtract profiled totals from unprofiled wall time, or interpret slot 25 as pure GPU work. Record that profile mode suppresses `br`.
3. To measure full decode phases, retain the existing host monotonic `STRATA_DECODE_TIMING` boundaries (including GPU-reach wait and CPU service). A future device-event experiment should be a separately reviewed source change: create timing events outside graph capture at explicitly defined stage boundaries, establish supported Xe/Level Zero event semantics and whether replayed graph nodes can record them, and compare with event-free wall measurements. Do not insert unsupported Level Zero event/tag commands into the captured graph; WN comments say those commands cannot be graph-captured. For per-kernel attribution, a supported external GPU trace/profiler can be evaluated in a separate diagnostic window, with its own overhead controls.

This audit does not implement event-based instrumentation and makes no claim about actual stamp overhead, B570 device-clock availability, or the profile’s measured values on hardware.

## Prior reports and primary references

Related local evidence: `round106-gdn-quiet-event-profiling-clock-and-error-contract.txt` (GDN event profiling semantics), `round194-ur-l0v2-submit-start-profiling-clock-contract.txt` (Level Zero submit-start clock contract), `round204-decode-pool-existing-counter-critical-path-seam.txt` (existing host counters), and `research-official-v0143-safe-parameter-campaign-round225-v1.txt` (separate profile and quiet measurement scopes).

Primary documentation:
- Intel oneAPI experimental clock extension: https://github.com/intel/llvm/blob/sycl/sycl/doc/extensions/experimental/sycl_ext_oneapi_clock.asciidoc — experimental API, device aspects, variable/non-time clock rate, no portable conversion.
- Intel oneAPI experimental graph extension: https://github.com/intel/llvm/blob/sycl/sycl/doc/extensions/experimental/sycl_ext_oneapi_graph.asciidoc — queue recording captures commands and dependencies as graph nodes; profiling/debugging interface is not part of the described extension.
- llama.cpp SYCL backend documentation: https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/docs/backend/SYCL.md — reviewed as an upstream backend reference; it does not provide a directly comparable per-stage device-clock decode attribution method, so no timing claims from it are imported here.
